answer: Think of your immune system as your body's security team, which has two main parts. The first is the "guards at the gate." Your skin, the mucus in your nose and throat, and your tears keep most germs out to begin with. If something gets past them, general-purpose white blood cells rush in within minutes to hours and swallow the intruders. That rush of defenders is what causes swelling, redness and heat around a cut [1][2]. The second part is the "specialist squad," and it takes a few days to get going. Some of these cells, called B cells, make antibodies, which work like tags that lock onto one particular germ. Others, called T cells, kill your own cells once they've been infected and help direct the fight [2][3]. The useful part is that the specialists remember germs they've already beaten. If the same germ comes back, your body fights it off faster and harder, often before you even feel sick. That memory is exactly what vaccines take advantage of [1][3]. The two parts work as a team, with the gate guards sounding the alarm that calls in the specialists [1].
